narrative: The model estimated your chance of failing the final year at 17%, which is low: it means the model leans strongly toward you passing, not failing. If remedial courses are being required, they should be understood as a precautionary support measure rather than a strong prediction that you will fail. In fact, the three most influential factors all pushed your prediction toward passing. The strongest was your record of no past class failures, which matches the average for students who passed. The second was your stated intention to continue to higher education; every passing student in the comparison group had that intention. The third was your mother’s secondary education level, a modest pass-leaning factor, though higher maternal education was more common among passers. These factors explain why your estimated fail risk is low rather than high. The main area to watch is attendance: you have 14 absences, far above the average of about 3.8 among students who passed. To improve your position, keep your no-failure record, protect your intention to continue studying, use your family support, and reduce absences. Because your family relationship quality was reported as bad, it may also help to seek a trusted adult or school counsellor for support. Treat the additional courses as a way to strengthen routines and attendance, not as proof that failure is likely.
